newsitem.title: GERMANY: Defence wants acquittal for East German spymaster.
newsitem.headline: Defence wants acquittal for East German spymaster.

text.p: Lawyers defending East Berlin's legendary spymaster Markus Wolf on trial for masterminding three kidnappings during the Cold War called on Tuesday for his acquittal.

The trial is the latest and possibly the last attempt to bring to punish the man who ran East Germany's foreign intelligence network for over 30 years after a 1993 treason conviction was overturned by Germany's high court in 1995.
Summing up, lawyer Wolfgang Roemmig said the statute of limitations on two charges of abduction had expired and that Wolf, 74, was not directly involved in the third case.
Prosecutors, who say Wolf engineered all three abductions and accuse him of coercion, causing injury and kidnapping, have demanded a three-and-a-half year jail sentence for him.
The court in the western city of Duesseldorf is due to deliver its verdict on May 27.
Wolf told the court he was being punished by what he called a political trial as a substitute for bringing to book former communist East German leaders.
He apologised for the practices of the East German secret service, but said they were similar to those in the west.
"I am sorry that because of East German espionage some people, through no fault of their own, found themselves in tragic circumstances," Wolf said.

Two weeks ago prosecutors dropped charges of treason and extortion against Wolf to speed up the trial, their latest bid to bring to book the elusive figure dubbed "the man without a face" by his Western counterparts, who for decades had little idea what he looked like.

Wolf was convicted of treason in the same Duesseldorf courtroom in 1993. But Germany's highest court overturned the decision in 1995, saying Wolf could not be convicted of spying on what was then a foreign country -- West Germany.
This time prosecutors charged Wolf with crimes under East German law during intelligence work in the 1950s and 1960s.

Wolf is charged with organising the kidnapping in 1959 of a Ministry for State Security (Stasi) official who had fled to West Germany and the abduction of a West Berlin secretary, who the authorities hoped to persuade to spy for the East.
Prosecutors said Wolf was also behind the arrest of an East German who the Stasi tried to force to take part in a plot against former chancellor Willy Brandt, then mayor of Berlin.
Roemmig said Wolf had not taken part in the 1959 kidnapping and said the other two cases were too old to try.

Wolf ran a network of around 4,000 foreign-based agents from his East Berlin headquarters. One of his biggest coups was planting "mole" Guenter Guillaume inside then chancellor Brandt's office -- leading to Brandt's resignation in 1974.
